newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian government faces uncertainties after split.
newsitem.headline: Indian government faces uncertainties after split.

text.p: A bitter split in Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party has exposed his two-month-old government to fresh uncertainties as it struggles to make key decisions, political analysts said on Monday.
They said Gujral's 13-party coalition government faced no serious threat to its survival but its functioning could be hampered by a division in his Janata Dal party.
A powerful dissident group on Saturday broke away from the party under the leadership of the Janata Dal's former president Laloo Prasad Yadav, who is mired in a corruption scandal.

Yadav said he would continue to support the centre-left government, where three of his supporters are ministers. But the ministers will have to resign if Yadav decides to support the government from outside without joining it.
"If it comes in as a coalition partner, there is no need to drop the ministers," political analyst B.G. Verghese said.
But Gujral might then need to soothe feelings in the rump Janata Dal by offering them more posts in the council of ministers, he said.

Gujral may also have trouble persuading the coalition's 15 parties, two of which are not included in government, to accept Yadav in the alliance after India's federal police indicted the former Janata Dal president in a $280 million embezzlement case.
Yadav, who is chief minister of the populous northern state of Bihar, says he is innocent and has repeatedly rejected calls from alliance partners to step down and face prosecution.
"We are all feeling uncomfortable," a senior United Front leader, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.
The alliance is already deeply divided over how to tackle a mounting oil subsidy bill and privatisation of state-run firms -- both considered essential to strengthen India's economy.
The United Front's powerful ally, Congress, may also flex its muscles and demand a position in the government to which it currently provides only external support in parliament, analysts said.
The coalition's 179 deputies depend on Congress's 140 in the 543-member lower house of parliament for their survival.

"If you cannot face mid-term elections and have no chances of forming a government of your own, your chances are better if you join it, and the Congress is in a stronger position now than it was earlier," said Pran Chopra, political analyst at the Centre For Policy Research.
"It is more than likely to force an entry into the government," he said.

Congress president Sitaram Kesri in April toppled the previous United Front government led by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda by abruptly withdrawing the party's backing but, reluctant to face mid-term polls, later agreed to support the alliance under a new leader.

"It would be surprising if the present confusion in the Front is not utilised by the Congress to up the ante and try for formal participation in the government," the Economic Times said in an editorial.
Other newspapers predicted greater political turmoil.

"The widespread disarray in the United Front resulting from the breakup of its largest constituent provides a fresh opportunity to the rejuvenated Congress," the Pioneer said. "Mr Sitaram Kesri has made no secret of his ambition to lead his party back to power."

"He (Kesri) is not getting any younger and certainly has his own agenda. Others may not share it but nobody will underestimate a second time his capacity to demolish a political set up, if not build a new one," the Business Standard said.
